newsitem.title: UK: UK's EMU caution said to cost 2 billion stg a year.
newsitem.headline: UK's EMU caution said to cost 2 billion stg a year.

text.p: Britain's tax payers are paying out two billion pounds ($3.1 billion) a year to finance the country's prevarication over whether to join a single European currency, economists and analysts say.

Caution within the ruling Conservative Party over whether to join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is keeping long-term market interest rates far higher than those in core European countries -- and Britons are forced to foot the bill.
And while some analysts say this is a fair price to pay for the option of joining the club, others say it is too much.
"The Treasury estimates that for every 10 basis points on gilt yields, it costs the tax payer 250 million pounds a year," said Adrian Owens, European Economist at Julius Baer investments in London.

With analysts judging that around 80 basis points of the premium on gilt yields over German Bund yields is down to the EMU factor, the cost of the "Euro option" is equivalent to one penny on the standard rate of income tax -- currently 24 pence in the pound. "It is a cost that it is difficult to justify. The government's deficit overshoot was three billion stg last year -- and if they had been signed up to EMU, the chances are that overshoot would only have been one billion," said Owens.

The spread or difference between 10-year gilt yields and their German counterparts is currently around 155 basis points -- meaning that the British government pays about 1.5 percentage point more interest on its debt.

But analysts said not all of that cost could be blamed on Britain's "opt-out" clause for EMU. Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel in London, said he would put "a good 70 or 80 basis points" of the spread down to Britain's wait-and-see stance on a single currency.
"So on each new bond that the government issues from now on, it will be paying 70/80 basis points more than it would otherwise have been," he said.
While analysts agreed there was a heavy price tag on having a choice about the Euro, some said the stance might turn out to have paid off later on, especially if the EMU party falls flat.

"There is no doubt we are paying higher rates than we would have been if we were seen as a more pro-active and enthusiastic candidate for EMU -- but that is not necessarily a bad thing in the long run," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC investment bank.

"If EMU starts to have problems -- if the structural problems of individual members' economies cause stresses and strains within the system -- you could even envisage a situation where bonds denominated in Euro would carry a slightly higher risk premium," he said.
"And countries outside the EMU system might then be viewed as safe havens."
Others say having a relatively weak currency in comparison with the mark can be good for the economy in the short term, helping to boost growth through higher exports.
The price may be worth paying, they say, for the benefit of maintaining sovereign control of the economy.

"There are costs and benefits -- some people would say that the last thing we need to do is have an exchange rate that is tied to the deutschemark," said Nigel Richardson, bond economist at Yamaichi International in London.
But analysts said taxpayers, whether willing to pay a price for non-commitment to the Euro or not, were unlikely to be out of pocket for long.
"I suspect that it will prove to be a temporary phenomonen," said CIBC's Cole. He said one of two things could bring about the end of the stinging premium paid at present.

Either the UK's stance on EMU would change along with a change of government, Cole said, or plans for EMU would crumble altogether, bring debt yields and hence interest rates in the rest of Europe back up to Bitain's level or above.
Yamaichi's Richardson agreed.
"Once a Labour government gets in -- assuming they do -- and sticks to its pro-EMU, more prudent fiscal policy, that spread will come in," he said.
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682 ($1=.6385 Pound)
